summary: Grand Passage light on the northern tip of Brier Island marks the north entrance to Grand Passage; lit in 1901, it was rebuilt in the 1960s, and Charles Buckman kept it from 1901 until 1940.

structures.note: 34 feet high to the vane, per the 1901 report
Parks Canada and the 2021 release give 1964; LighthouseFriends says the original was demolished in 1968

access.note: Grounds open, tower closed (LighthouseFriends). Parking beside the light; the last kilometre is gravel from Westport.

facts.agency: Canadian Coast Guard (LighthouseFriends); the 2021 announcement lists it among lights managed by new, non-federal owners, unnamed

events.note: Put in operation 12 January 1901 on the north point of Brier Island; fixed red light, seventh-order dioptric
Fog bell established by the station, supported by a framework beside the tower (LighthouseFriends dates it 1903; the report for the year to 30 June 1904 says it had been established)
Dwelling houses erected at the two light stations on Brier Island, one of them Grand Passage; contract $3,150 (report, OCR reads 'E. 0. Bowers'; LighthouseFriends prints E. C. Bowers)
Three-masted schooner Allen Greene of Deer Isle, Maine, lost in Grand Passage in a northwest gale, 17 March 1911; cook drowned
Bottle picked up by keeper Charles Buckman in November 1914, with a note on the back of a memorandum leaf: 'August 8th, 1914 - German war ship off Coast of Maine.'
Assistant's post dropped within months of Wickerson Lent's arrival, LighthouseFriends says because the light was being automated
Rebuilt with a fog alarm building attached (Parks Canada); constructed in 1964 to replace the original 1901 lighthouse (2021 release)
LighthouseFriends: the original lighthouse was demolished in 1968 and replaced by the current one (conflicts with 1964)
Designated a heritage lighthouse under the Heritage Lighthouse Protection Act in December 2021

wrecks.outcome: Three-masted schooner of Deer Isle, Maine, lost in Grand Passage in a northwest gale; the cook, Ambrose N. Ames of Rockland, was washed overboard and drowned; the captain and five crew reached the shore of Brier Island. The newspapers do not connect the light or its keeper with the rescue

notes_for_editor: Conflicts left open in the story: rebuilt tower 1964 (Parks Canada, 2021 announcement) against demolition of the original in 1968 (LighthouseFriends); the station record gives 1964 and 1965. Ownership is disputed: LighthouseFriends says the Canadian Coast Guard owns it; the 2021 announcement says it is managed by a non-federal owner, unnamed; the Parks statement says the Coast Guard uses the former dwelling. The 2021 announcement describes the passage as running between Brier Island and 'the western shore of St. Mary's Bay', while LighthouseFriends and the 1911 Daily Kennebec Journal say Long Island; the story now states both. The dwelling contract: the 1905 report (scan 34, printed 29) names the contractor as 'Mr. E. 0. Bowers, of Westport, N.S.' in OCR (zero for O); LighthouseFriends prints 'E. C. Bowers'. The initial was matched on OCR text only and not checked on the page image. The 1910 keepers' table (1911v45i13p21_0744, scan 257, printed 255) has 'Chas. Buckman' appointed 7 January 1901, but the station column is not legible in the OCR; it is not used as a source for the station; check the image if wanted. The 1901 report is cited to scan page 74, because the printed page is not confirmed by the OCR index. Keeper gap: no head keeper is named between Buckman's death (1940) and Lent (1977); the sources read do not fill it. Wickerson Lent and Lawrence F. Welch are named in public role only; family details printed by LighthouseFriends are left out. The Allen Greene loss: the Kennebec Journal OCR garbles its date line, so 17 March from the Evening Star dispatch is used. The newspaper search found two pages from 1911 only; no other wreck or rescue at this station was found, and the newspapers do not link the light or its keeper to the rescue. Search budget: one websearch.py call, two loc.gov pages read, and the newspaper search with two hits.
